title: Analysis and Control of the Microstructure of Electrodeposited Alkali-Metals in “Anode-free” Solid-State Batteries using Electron-Backscatter Diffraction with and without Interlayers
content: Lithium metal, when used as an anode material, can significantly enhance the energy and power density of solid-state batteries [1]. However, issues such as local contact loss and dendrite formation disrupt homogeneous stripping and plating and thereby limit the cycling rate. Previous studies have demonstrated that the lithium metal microstructure plays a crucial role in determining the electrochemical performance, particularly in terms of stripping capacity before pore formation occurs [2]. Further, Solid-state batteries (SSBs) without an alkali metal reservoir are being extensively studied for their potential to achieve unparalleled energy densities while eliminating the need to handle reactive and inherently hazardous alkali metal foils [3-5]. Despite its anticipated impact on electrochemical performance, the microstructure of electrodeposited lithium (or sodium) has not yet been visualized at all. A multitude of reasons impede the analysis of alkali metal microstructures, being the buried nature of solid|solid interfaces, strong tendency of degradation of alkali metal surfaces and low material density.
